questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is admitted with 4 days of fever to 104.5 F, nonproductive cough, headache, and watery diarrhea. He stayed at a hotel one week ago, and two other guests from the same hotel have been admitted with pneumonia. Serum sodium is 126 mEq/L. Chest radiograph shows a dense lower lobe consolidation, and a urine antigen test is positive. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

explanation.summary: Hotel or cooling-tower exposure with high fever, diarrhea, hyponatremia, a lobar pattern, and a positive urine antigen points to Legionella pneumophila.
explanation.whyCorrect: L. pneumophila is acquired from contaminated water aerosols such as hotel cooling towers, and outbreaks cluster among people at one site. Fever above 104 F occurs in about 20% of patients, watery diarrhea in 25-50%, and hyponatremia (sodium below 131) is a recognized clinical clue. Unlike the other atypicals, Legionnaires' disease commonly shows a lobar pattern on imaging, and the urine antigen test is the rapid confirmatory test described for this organism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. pneumoniae causes mild atypical pneumonia with diffuse patchy opacities and is diagnosed by nucleic acid amplification, not urine antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C. psittaci requires contact with infected birds and is not transmitted by contaminated water systems.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M. pneumoniae causes gradual, mild walking pneumonia with interstitial infiltrates and is not detected by a urine antigen test.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae causes lobar pneumonia but is not linked to cooling-tower outbreaks, diarrhea, or hyponatremia in this brick.

questions.topicName: Atypical Bacteria

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student has had a dry, hacking cough, low-grade fever, malaise, and headache for 3 weeks. Several students on his dormitory floor have had similar illnesses. He looks well and walks into clinic unassisted, but chest radiograph shows streaky, patchy interstitial infiltrates that appear worse than his symptoms suggest. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

explanation.summary: Mild, gradual-onset 'walking pneumonia' in a young adult with dormitory clustering and radiographic findings out of proportion to symptoms is classic for Mycoplasma pneumoniae.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. pneumoniae is a leading cause of community-acquired and atypical pneumonia in children and young adults, and outbreaks occur in college dorms, military barracks, and daycares. It is often called walking pneumonia because the illness is mild and self-limiting. Lung involvement frequently appears more severe than the patient's symptoms suggest, with streaky or patchy interstitial infiltrates on imaging.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. psittaci requires contact with infected birds, which is not described here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Legionnaires' disease typically affects patients over 40 and presents with high fever and a lobar pattern, not a mild 3-week course in a well-appearing student.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. aureus is listed as a cause of severe pneumonia in ICU patients, not mild ambulatory illness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae causes rapid-onset illness with a productive cough and lobar consolidation.

questions.topicName: Atypical Bacteria

questions.stem: A 28-year-old pet-store employee who recently began caring for newly arrived macaws and cockatoos develops 10 days of fever, fatigue, sore throat, and a dry cough. Chest radiograph shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

explanation.summary: Atypical pneumonia in a person with occupational bird exposure is psittacosis, caused by Chlamydia psittaci.
explanation.whyCorrect: C. psittaci is named for its association with psittacine birds such as parrots, cockatoos, and macaws. It is not transmitted person to person; infection follows contact with infected birds, so cases occur in people who work around birds or keep them as pets. Its clinical picture is otherwise indistinguishable from C. pneumoniae, ranging from flu-like illness to severe pneumonia with high fever.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. pneumoniae presents identically but spreads person to person by respiratory droplets, with no bird link.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H. influenzae is a typical pathogen causing productive cough and is not bird associated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: L. pneumophila comes from contaminated water aerosols and usually causes higher fever with a lobar pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: M. pneumoniae spreads person to person and has no zoonotic reservoir described here.

questions.topicName: Atypical Bacteria

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy is brought in with fever and a rash that began on his face and spread to his trunk. Over the past day he has developed painful erosions of the lips and oral mucosa, and examination shows target-like lesions with skin detachment over about 10% of the body surface. He had a respiratory illness with a dry cough 2 weeks ago and takes no medications. Which of the following organisms most likely triggered his condition?

explanation.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the most frequently identified infectious trigger of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, especially in children and adolescents.
explanation.whyCorrect: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and its more severe form, toxic epidermal necrolysis, involve painful rashes and blisters of skin and mucous membranes at sites such as the lips, nose, eyes, and genitals. The mechanism is an immune-mediated response triggered by certain infections and medications that causes cell death and detachment of the epidermis and mucous membranes. Although medications are the most common cause overall, among infections M. pneumoniae is the one most often identified, particularly in this age group.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. pneumoniae causes atypical pneumonia but is not identified as a common trigger of Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C. psittaci can disseminate to liver, heart, and brain, but is not the typical trigger of this reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: L. pneumophila causes severe pneumonia with gastrointestinal symptoms, not this mucocutaneous syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae is a typical pneumonia pathogen and is not linked to this syndrome here.

questions.topicName: Atypical Bacteria

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with 2 weeks of gradual-onset malaise and a dry cough is treated with high-dose amoxicillin for presumed pneumonia. She shows no improvement after several days, and sputum culture on routine media grows nothing. Which of the following features of the responsible organism best explains the failure of therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It alternates between elementary and reticulate bodies

choices.label: B
choices.text: It blocks phagosome-lysosome fusion inside macrophages

choices.label: C
choices.text: It has no cell wall for the drug to act on

choices.label: D
choices.text: It hides within a large cytoplasmic inclusion body

choices.label: E
choices.text: It secretes an enzyme that destroys the drug

explanation.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae has no cell wall, so antibiotics that inhibit cell wall synthesis are inherently ineffective.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. pneumoniae is the tiniest free-living organism capable of self-replication and lacks a cell wall entirely, which also makes it pleomorphic. Because beta-lactams work by inhibiting cell wall synthesis, they have no target in this organism. Atypical pneumonia is in fact defined as pneumonia caused by non-classical pathogens that do not respond to beta-lactam antibiotics.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The elementary and reticulate body cycle belongs to Chlamydia species, not Mycoplasma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking phagosome-lysosome fusion is how Legionella survives in macrophages and does not explain beta-lactam failure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Growth inside a large inclusion body is a Chlamydia feature, not a Mycoplasma feature.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Beta-lactamase production is not described as the mechanism of resistance for this organism.

questions.topicName: Atypical Bacteria

questions.stem: A respiratory isolate from a young adult with atypical pneumonia will grow only on media supplemented with cholesterol, and after prolonged incubation the colonies have a characteristic fried-egg appearance. Which of the following organisms is most consistent with these findings?

explanation.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae requires sterols in its culture medium and forms fried-egg colonies.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sterols are present in the M. pneumoniae cell membrane, a feature rare among bacteria, and culturing the organism therefore requires that sterols be present in the media. In culture the colonies take on a fried-egg appearance, and the memory hook offered is that eggs contain cholesterol, linking the colony shape to the growth requirement.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. pneumoniae is an obligate intracellular organism that requires cell culture rather than enriched agar.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C. psittaci likewise grows only inside living host cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: L. pneumophila needs iron and cysteine on buffered charcoal yeast extract agar, not sterols.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae grows readily on standard laboratory media without added sterols.

questions.topicName: Atypical Bacteria

questions.stem: A previously healthy 35-year-old is diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia and will be treated as an outpatient. Besides Streptococcus pneumoniae and respiratory viruses, which of the following groups of organisms are among the most common causes of pneumonia in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Klebsiella pneumoniae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Legionella species

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gram-negative bacilli, Staphylococcus aureus, and Chlamydia psittaci

choices.label: C
choices.text: Legionella species, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Haemophilus influenzae

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Staphylococcus aureus, Legionella species, and gram-negative bacilli

explanation.summary: Outpatient community-acquired pneumonia is most often caused by S. pneumoniae, M. pneumoniae, C. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, and respiratory viruses.
explanation.whyCorrect: The microbial causes of community-acquired pneumonia differ by site of care. In outpatients, the listed organisms are S. pneumoniae, M. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, C. pneumoniae, and respiratory viruses. Legionella species appear among hospitalized non-ICU and ICU patients, and S. aureus and gram-negative bacilli appear in the ICU group, reflecting more severe disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. trachomatis causes urethritis and eye infections rather than community-acquired pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gram-negative bacilli and S. aureus are ICU-associated, and C. psittaci requires bird exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Legionella is a hospitalized-patient pathogen here, and C. trachomatis is not a pneumonia pathogen in this list.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These are the organisms listed for ICU patients with severe pneumonia, not ambulatory patients.

questions.topicName: Atypical Bacteria

questions.stem: Mycoplasma pneumoniae must first attach to ciliated epithelial cells of the lower airway before it can enter cells and establish infection. Which of the following mediates this attachment?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flagella and pili on the bacterial surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: Surface proteins of the elementary body

explanation.summary: P1 is the virulence factor by which M. pneumoniae binds ciliated respiratory epithelium.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. pneumoniae attaches to respiratory epithelial cells using the virulence factor P1, which binds ciliated epithelial cells in the lungs and facilitates entry of the bacteria into cells. After attachment there is roughly a 2 to 3 week incubation period before the gradual onset of symptoms, which is why the illness is easy to miss early.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A capsule is not among the virulence factors described for this organism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Flagella and pili are how L. pneumophila attaches to respiratory epithelium and macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M. pneumoniae has no cell wall and is not described as using an O antigen for adherence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Elementary bodies are the infectious form of Chlamydia species, not a Mycoplasma structure.

questions.topicName: Atypical Bacteria

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man shares a dormitory room with a student who has just been diagnosed with Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection. If he becomes infected, approximately how long after exposure would symptoms be expected to begin?

explanation.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae has a roughly 2 to 3 week incubation period followed by gradual onset of symptoms.
explanation.whyCorrect: After P1-mediated attachment to ciliated epithelium, there is approximately a 2 to 3 week incubation period before symptoms begin gradually. This long incubation and insidious onset contrast with the 2 to 10 day incubation and rapid progression seen with Legionnaires' disease, and they help explain why outbreaks in closed settings unfold slowly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: One to two days is far shorter than the incubation described for this organism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Months-long latency is not described for M. pneumoniae.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Four to six days approximates the Legionella range, which is 2 to 10 days.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An incubation of hours would suggest a toxin-mediated illness, not Mycoplasma infection.

questions.topicName: Atypical Bacteria

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman has a 10-day history of dry cough, low-grade fever, and headache, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection is suspected. Which of the following tests provides the most accurate and rapid confirmation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cold agglutinin titer on chilled serum

choices.label: B
choices.text: Culture on buffered charcoal yeast extract agar

choices.label: D
choices.text: PCR performed on a respiratory specimen

explanation.summary: PCR is the most accurate and rapid way to diagnose Mycoplasma pneumoniae.
explanation.whyCorrect: None of the clinical manifestations of M. pneumoniae infection are distinct enough to separate it from other atypical pneumonias, and the organism grows only on specialized Eaton agar over weeks. As with viruses, PCR can be performed on patient samples, and it is explicitly the most accurate and rapid way to establish the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cold agglutination is nonspecific and is no longer recommended now that better tests exist.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Buffered charcoal yeast extract agar is the medium for Legionella, and Mycoplasma requires sterol-containing media.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The organism has no cell wall and is not seen on Gram stain of sputum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The urine antigen test described in this brick detects Legionella, not Mycoplasma.

questions.topicName: Atypical Bacteria

questions.stem: A resident proposes mixing a patient's serum with red blood cells and chilling the mixture to support a presumptive diagnosis of Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection. Which of the following is the best reason this test is no longer recommended?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cannot be performed once antibiotics are started

choices.label: B
choices.text: It detects only a single serotype of the organism

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is nonspecific; other conditions cause agglutination

choices.label: D
choices.text: It requires living host cells to propagate the organism

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires several weeks of incubation to be read

explanation.summary: Cold agglutination testing has been abandoned because it is not specific and better tests are now available.
explanation.whyCorrect: Historically, cold agglutination tests supported a diagnosis of M. pneumoniae: patient serum was mixed with red blood cells and chilled, and antibodies caused the cells to clump. Combined with the clinical picture it served as a quick presumptive test, but it is not specific because other conditions also cause cold agglutination. Since more specific tests such as PCR are now available, cold agglutination is no longer recommended.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Prior antibiotic use is not the stated limitation of this test.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Detection of only one serotype describes the Legionella urine antigen test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Requiring living host cells describes Chlamydia culture, not a serum agglutination assay.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Weeks of incubation describes Eaton agar culture, not the agglutination test, which is quick.

questions.topicName: Atypical Bacteria

questions.stem: A 21-year-old with patchy interstitial infiltrates has sputum and blood cultures that show no growth after 48 hours, and the team concludes the illness must be viral. Which of the following best explains the negative cultures if Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It circulates only in blood and never in the airway

choices.label: B
choices.text: It grows only within living host cells and cannot be cultured

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is destroyed by the transport medium used for sputum

choices.label: D
choices.text: It needs iron and cysteine that standard media lack

choices.label: E
choices.text: It needs specialized Eaton agar and weeks of incubation

explanation.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes culture-negative pneumonia because it requires specialized Eaton agar and weeks of growth.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. pneumoniae can be cultured only on specialized Eaton agar, which is not typically stocked in clinical laboratories, and the culture takes weeks. As a result the organism produces culture-negative pneumonia, which makes a virus appear to be the cause and contributes to the infection being underdiagnosed. Rapid PCR testing is what resolves the picture.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The organism infects the respiratory tract and is transmitted by respiratory droplets.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Obligate intracellular growth requiring cell culture describes Chlamydia species.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Destruction by transport medium is not the explanation given for negative cultures.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron and cysteine requirements belong to the fastidious Legionella pneumophila.

questions.topicName: Atypical Bacteria

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman from Connecticut comes to the clinic in late June with fatigue, low-grade fever, and aching joints. She went camping in the woods 10 days ago. On her thigh is a red patch about 9 cm across that has slowly enlarged over several days and now has a pale center surrounded by a red ring. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: An expanding bull's-eye rash (erythema migrans) after a woodland tick exposure in the Northeast is pathognomonic for Lyme disease caused by Borrelia burgdorferi.
explanation.whyCorrect: Erythema migrans is a red rash that gradually expands outward from the bite site and can take on a bull's-eye appearance; it is pathognomonic for Lyme disease. Combined with fatigue, fever, joint aches, and exposure in the northeastern United States, where Lyme disease is most frequent, this points to B. burgdorferi transmitted by Ixodes scapularis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: E. chaffeensis causes a nonspecific febrile illness (fever, headache, myalgia, nausea); a pathognomonic expanding bull's-eye rash is not its feature.
whyWrongByChoice.C: E. ewingii is another agent of ehrlichiosis, which presents with nonspecific fever and myalgia rather than erythema migrans.
whyWrongByChoice.D: E. muris eauclairensis causes ehrlichiosis, a febrile illness without the hallmark bull's-eye rash of Lyme disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: R. rickettsii causes a maculopapular rash that begins on the wrists and ankles and spreads to the trunk, not a single expanding bull's-eye lesion.

questions.topicName: Bacterial Tick-borne Diseases

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy from Oklahoma is brought to the physician in June with 3 days of high fever, severe headache, vomiting, and muscle aches. His mother removed a tick from his scalp 6 days ago after he played near a wooded creek. He has no rash yet. If the most likely diagnosis is correct, which of the following best describes how his rash will most likely evolve?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single red patch at the bite site that expands with central clearing

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maculopapular spots on the trunk that then spread to the wrists and ankles

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maculopapular spots on wrists and ankles that then spread to the trunk

choices.label: D
choices.text: Petechiae confined to the bite site that never extend beyond it

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several expanding ring-shaped patches on skin far from the bite site

explanation.summary: The RMSF rash is maculopapular, typically beginning on the wrists, ankles, palms, and soles and spreading toward the trunk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fever, severe headache, vomiting, and myalgia after a tick bite in a south-central state suggest Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Its maculopapular rash, a sign of vasculitis, characteristically starts around the wrists, ankles, palms, and soles and then spreads toward the torso, often appearing 2-4 days after the fever begins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An expanding bull's-eye patch at the bite site is erythema migrans of Lyme disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This reverses the RMSF pattern; the rash begins peripherally and moves centrally.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The RMSF rash is not limited to the bite site; it spreads from the extremities to the trunk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Multiple erythema migrans lesions at distant sites reflect early disseminated (stage 2) Lyme disease.

questions.topicName: Bacterial Tick-borne Diseases

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man from Missouri has 5 days of fever, headache, muscle aches, and nausea that began about 9 days after he pulled a tick off his waistband while hunting. He has no rash. A peripheral blood smear shows mulberry-shaped clusters of bacteria inside cytoplasmic vacuoles of white blood cells. These clusters are most likely found within which of the following cell types?

explanation.summary: Ehrlichia spp. have a tropism for mononuclear phagocytes, where they form mulberry-shaped morulae.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ehrlichiosis presents with fever, headache, malaise, myalgia, and nausea 5-14 days after a tick bite. Ehrlichia spp. are small gram-negative obligate intracellular bacteria with a tropism for mononuclear phagocytes such as monocytes and macrophages; clusters within vacuoles form mulberry-shaped aggregates called morulae.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ehrlichiosis usually lacks a rash, and the organism's tropism is for mononuclear phagocytes, not skin cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ehrlichia does not infect red blood cells; it resides in mononuclear phagocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelets are not the host cell; morulae form within vacuoles of mononuclear phagocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Endothelial cells are the target of Rickettsia rickettsii, producing vasculitis, not intraleukocyte morulae.

questions.topicName: Bacterial Tick-borne Diseases

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man from Massachusetts comes to the emergency department because he cannot close his right eye and the right side of his mouth droops. Six weeks ago he had an enlarging red rash on his calf after a camping trip, which faded without treatment. He now reports shooting pains in his arms. An ECG shows atrioventricular block. Which of the following processes best explains his current findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune response persisting after completed antibiotic therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endothelial infection producing widespread vasculitis and clotting

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infection of mononuclear phagocytes with formation of morulae

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sensitization to a carbohydrate found in mammalian red meat

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spread of spirochetes from the skin to distant tissues

explanation.summary: Facial palsy, shooting pains, and heart block weeks after erythema migrans indicate early disseminated (stage 2) Lyme disease, caused by dissemination of B. burgdorferi.
explanation.whyCorrect: Stage 2 Lyme disease occurs weeks to months after the bite, when localized skin infection by B. burgdorferi disseminates. It produces multiple rashes, meningitis, facial (Bell) palsy, generalized shooting pains, numbness or tingling, pericarditis, and heart block, usually at the atrioventricular node.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A possible autoimmune response is proposed for post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome; this patient was never treated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Endothelial infection with systemic vasculitis is the mechanism of Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Morulae in mononuclear phagocytes characterize ehrlichiosis, which rarely causes complications.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alpha-gal sensitization follows Lone star tick bites and causes allergic reactions to red meat, not palsy or heart block.

questions.topicName: Bacterial Tick-borne Diseases

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman from New Hampshire has had fatigue and migrating joint aches for 5 weeks. She recalls a ring-shaped rash on her back in early summer that resolved. Her physician wants to confirm infection with the spirochete transmitted by the blacklegged tick. Which of the following is the recommended diagnostic approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Culture of synovial fluid on routine agar read within 48 hours

choices.label: B
choices.text: ELISA for IgM and IgG, confirmed by a secondary ELISA or Western blot

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gram stain of a skin biopsy taken from the site of the old rash

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paired IFA titers showing a fourfold rise in IgG over 2-4 weeks

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peripheral blood smear examined for intracytoplasmic morulae

explanation.summary: Lyme disease is diagnosed by ELISA for IgM and IgG against B. burgdorferi, confirmed by a secondary ELISA or Western blot.
explanation.whyCorrect: Staining and culture are not consistent enough to diagnose Lyme disease, so the recommended pathway is detection of IgM and IgG antibodies by ELISA with confirmation by a secondary ELISA or Western blot. At 5 weeks, antibodies are detectable in most patients (70-90% beyond 2-4 weeks).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Culture of B. burgdorferi is difficult and takes 6-8 weeks; it is not the recommended pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Spirochetes do not stain well by Gram stain, and staining is not consistent enough for diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Paired IFA with a fourfold IgG rise is the gold standard serologic test for RMSF, not Lyme disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Morulae in mononuclear phagocytes are a feature of ehrlichiosis.

questions.topicName: Bacterial Tick-borne Diseases

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman from Vermont comes to the clinic with a 7-cm red patch with central clearing on her shoulder, fatigue, and low-grade fever. She removed an engorged tick from the same spot 8 days ago. An ELISA for antibodies to Borrelia burgdorferi drawn today is negative. Which of the following is the best interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diagnosis should await culture of a biopsy from the lesion margin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Infection is excluded because the screening ELISA is negative

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infection is still likely; diagnosis early rests on history and the rash

choices.label: D
choices.text: The lesion is unlikely to be erythema migrans since serology is negative

choices.label: E
choices.text: The result reflects cross-reacting antibodies to commensal spirochetes

explanation.summary: Early in Lyme disease antibodies are detected in only 20-50% of patients, so history and erythema migrans are the most helpful diagnostic tools.
explanation.whyCorrect: It takes weeks for antibody levels to rise to detectable levels: antibodies are found in only 20-50% of patients in the first 2 weeks versus 70-90% later. A negative early ELISA therefore does not rule out infection, and a tick bite history with erythema migrans, which is pathognomonic, is the most helpful basis for diagnosis early on.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Culture is difficult and takes 6-8 weeks, making it impractical for diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Early serology has low sensitivity (20-50%), so a negative test does not exclude Lyme disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Erythema migrans is a clinical diagnosis; seronegativity is expected this early and does not change what the rash is.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cross-reactive antibodies to microbiota spirochetes would cause false positives, not a negative result.

questions.topicName: Bacterial Tick-borne Diseases

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man from Arkansas has 6 days of fever, severe headache, and myalgia. Four days into the illness a maculopapular rash appeared on his wrists and ankles, later spreading to his palms, soles, and trunk; it is now becoming petechial. He removed a tick after yard work 10 days ago. Infection of which of the following cell types best explains the rash?

explanation.summary: R. rickettsii has a strong tropism for endothelial cells; their infection causes widespread vasculitis, which produces the rash.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Omp proteins facilitate uptake of R. rickettsii into cells, and the organism has a strong tropism for endothelial cells. Endothelial infection leads to widespread vasculitis, producing the rash and, in severe cases, clotting, edema, and tissue necrosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The rash results from vasculitis of infected blood vessels, not from infection of skin epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.B: R. rickettsii does not target red cells and is not commonly seen in blood until severe disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatocytes are not the organism's primary target; its tropism is for endothelium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mononuclear phagocytes are the target of Ehrlichia spp., which form morulae and usually cause no rash.

questions.topicName: Bacterial Tick-borne Diseases

questions.stem: A public health officer reviews annual surveillance of tick-borne illnesses in the United States. One disease accounts for far more cases than any other, but a different one causes the most deaths. Which of the following is the most common cause of fatal tick-borne disease in the United States?

explanation.summary: RMSF, caused by R. rickettsii, is the most common cause of fatal tick-borne disease in the U.S., although Lyme disease causes many more cases.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lyme disease is the most common tick-borne disease in the U.S., but its mortality is much lower. Death from Rocky Mountain spotted fever is rare, yet it remains the leading cause of tick-borne death because systemic vasculitis can cause cerebral edema, respiratory compromise, tissue necrosis, and multiorgan failure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-gal syndrome is an allergy to red meat after Lone star tick bites, not the leading cause of tick-borne death.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Complications of ehrlichiosis are rare according to the lecture.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lyme disease is the most common tick-borne disease, but its mortality is much lower than that of RMSF.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PTLDS causes lingering pain, cognitive issues, and fatigue after therapy, not death.

questions.topicName: Bacterial Tick-borne Diseases

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman from Tennessee is started on antibiotics for suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever after developing fever, headache, and a rash that began on her ankles. Her physician wants to confirm the diagnosis using the gold standard serologic method. Which of the following testing strategies is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single IgG titer drawn on the first day of symptoms

choices.label: B
choices.text: A single IgM titer drawn on the first day of symptoms

choices.label: C
choices.text: Culture of venous blood on routine laboratory agar

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gram stain of a peripheral blood smear

choices.label: E
choices.text: IgG IFA on a week-1 serum and on a serum 2-4 weeks later

explanation.summary: The gold standard for RMSF is IFA on two paired serum samples showing a fourfold rise in IgG titer.
explanation.whyCorrect: The gold standard serologic test for RMSF is the indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA) with R. rickettsii antigen on paired sera: one drawn as early as possible (preferably in the first week) and one 2-4 weeks later, looking for a fourfold rise. A single sample is hard to interpret because titers can persist from past exposure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The first IgG titer is typically low or negative, and one sample cannot show a rising titer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgM is less specific and prone to false positives, and a single sample is difficult to interpret.
whyWrongByChoice.C: R. rickettsii is obligate intracellular and cannot be cultured on agar.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The organism stains poorly by Gram stain and is rarely found in blood until severe disease.

questions.topicName: Bacterial Tick-borne Diseases

questions.stem: A physician in North Carolina counsels several patients about which of them face the highest risk of severe illness if infected by Rickettsia rickettsii. Which of the following patients is at greatest risk of severe disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 15-year-old girl who is a healthy competitive swimmer

choices.label: B
choices.text: A 35-year-old man who had treated Lyme disease two years earlier

choices.label: C
choices.text: A 35-year-old man with alpha-gal syndrome after a Lone star bite

choices.label: D
choices.text: A 35-year-old man with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: A 45-year-old woman with seasonal allergies and no other illness

explanation.summary: Children under 10, immunocompromised patients, and those with G6PD deficiency are at highest risk for severe RMSF.
explanation.whyCorrect: The lecture identifies three groups at greatest risk for severe Rocky Mountain spotted fever: children younger than 10 years, the immunocompromised, and patients with G6PD deficiency. The other patients listed have no stated risk factor for severe disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The high-risk pediatric group is children younger than 10 years.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Prior Lyme disease is not a listed risk factor for severe RMSF.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpha-gal allergy is not a risk factor for severe RMSF.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No listed risk factor applies; severe disease clusters in young children, the immunocompromised, and G6PD deficiency.

questions.topicName: Bacterial Tick-borne Diseases

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man from Tennessee has 4 days of fever and malaise but no rash and no recalled tick bite. A single serum sample drawn today shows an elevated IgM titer against Rickettsia rickettsii antigen; no other antibody class was measured. Which of the following is the best interpretation of this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It confirms acute infection, and no further testing is required

choices.label: B
choices.text: It excludes the infection, because IgM appears only after the rash

choices.label: C
choices.text: It indicates a prior infection that has left the patient immune

choices.label: D
choices.text: It indicates Lyme disease, since IgM cross-reacts with spirochetes

choices.label: E
choices.text: May reflect past exposure; needs concurrent IgG and a later sample

explanation.summary: IgM is less specific than IgG and titers persist from past or related exposures, so a lone IgM must be paired with IgG and a convalescent sample.
explanation.whyCorrect: IgM rises at about the same time as IgG near the end of the first week, is less specific, and is more likely to give a false positive, so IgM requests should include a concurrent IgG. Titers can stay elevated for months to years, and up to 10% of healthy people in some areas have elevated titers from past exposure to R. rickettsii or related organisms. A fourfold rise between paired samples gives the best evidence.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A single IgM titer is not specific enough to confirm acute RMSF.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgM rises near the end of the first week regardless of rash; a positive result does not exclude infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An isolated IgM result cannot establish past infection or immunity; paired IgG testing is needed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cross-reaction with commensal spirochetes is an issue in Lyme serology, not a reason to diagnose Lyme here.

questions.topicName: Bacterial Tick-borne Diseases

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman from New York removes a tick from her thigh after gardening. She brings it to the clinic, where it is identified as Ixodes scapularis. Infection with which of the following pairs of tick-borne diseases is she at risk of from this tick species?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lyme disease and Rocky Mountain spotted fever

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rocky Mountain spotted fever and alpha-gal syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rocky Mountain spotted fever and ehrlichiosis

explanation.summary: Ixodes scapularis transmits both B. burgdorferi (Lyme disease) and Ehrlichia spp. (ehrlichiosis).
explanation.whyCorrect: The blacklegged (deer) tick, Ixodes scapularis, is the vector of Lyme disease. Ehrlichiosis is spread by the Lone star tick (Amblyomma americanum) and also by Ixodes scapularis, the same vector that transmits Lyme disease. RMSF is carried by Dermacentor and Rhipicephalus ticks, and alpha-gal syndrome follows Lone star tick bites.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This pair fits the Lone star tick (Amblyomma americanum), not Ixodes scapularis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: RMSF is transmitted by the American dog tick, Rocky Mountain wood tick, and brown dog tick, not by Ixodes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neither is linked to Ixodes; RMSF is spread by Dermacentor and Rhipicephalus, alpha-gal by the Lone star tick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ehrlichiosis can come from Ixodes, but RMSF is carried by Dermacentor and Rhipicephalus ticks.

questions.topicName: Bacterial Tick-borne Diseases

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has fever, flank pain, and costovertebral angle tenderness. Blood and urine cultures grow Escherichia coli, and susceptibility testing shows the isolate produces an extended-spectrum β-lactamase. Which of the following is the most reliable treatment?

explanation.summary: Carbapenems are the most reliable treatment for ESBL-producing bacteria.
explanation.whyCorrect: ESBLs are β-lactamase enzymes that degrade other β-lactam antibiotics. Carbapenems such as meropenem resist these enzymes and are considered the most reliable treatment for infections caused by ESBL-producing bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aminopenicillins, even with a β-lactamase inhibitor, do not provide reliable coverage against ESBL-producing Enterobacterales.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ESBL enzymes degrade other β-lactam antibiotics such as cephalosporins, so ceftriaxone is not reliable here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Piperacillin-tazobactam is broad but should not be considered reliably active against ESBL-producing pathogens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vancomycin has no gram-negative coverage at all.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and indications-2 β-lactams and 30s Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man who has been mechanically ventilated for 6 days develops fever, purulent tracheal secretions, and a new infiltrate. Sputum culture grows Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The team plans to use a carbapenem. Which of the following agents would be inappropriate for this organism?

explanation.summary: Ertapenem is the carbapenem that does not cover Pseudomonas, Enterococcus, or Acinetobacter (PEA).
explanation.whyCorrect: Most carbapenems (meropenem, doripenem, imipenem/cilastatin) cover most gram-negative bacteria. The key exception is ertapenem, which lacks coverage against Pseudomonas, Enterococcus, and Acinetobacter: 'ErtAPenem does not cover PEA.'

whyWrongByChoice.A: Doripenem is among the carbapenems that cover most gram-negative bacteria, including Pseudomonas; the exception is ertapenem.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Imipenem/cilastatin is a carbapenem with broad gram-negative activity; it is not the exception the lecture flags.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Meropenem covers most gram-negative bacteria, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Piperacillin-tazobactam has activity against susceptible Pseudomonas aeruginosa, so it would not be inappropriate.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and indications-2 β-lactams and 30s Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has a complicated urinary tract infection, and urine culture grows Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The team wants a β-lactam that acts on this aerobic gram-negative bacillus but has no gram-positive or anaerobic activity, so that his normal microbiota is disturbed as little as possible. Which of the following best fits?

explanation.summary: Aztreonam, a monobactam, covers aerobic gram-negative bacilli including Pseudomonas but spares gram-positive and anaerobic flora.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aztreonam has activity against susceptible aerobic gram-negative bacteria, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, but no activity against gram-positive or anaerobic organisms. That narrow profile makes it useful for gram-negative bacillary infections without disrupting the patient's microbiota.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aminopenicillins do not reliably cover Pseudomonas aeruginosa and have gram-positive activity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ertapenem is broad-spectrum and, unlike other carbapenems, does not cover Pseudomonas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Meropenem covers Pseudomonas but also covers gram-positive organisms broadly, so it does not spare the microbiota.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Piperacillin-tazobactam covers Pseudomonas but also has broad gram-positive and anaerobic activity.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and indications-2 β-lactams and 30s Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy develops fever, headache, and a petechial rash that began on his wrists and ankles about a week after a camping trip during which several ticks were removed from his scalp. A rickettsial infection is suspected. Which of the following is the first-line treatment?

explanation.summary: Doxycycline is the first-line treatment for Rickettsiae.
explanation.whyCorrect: Doxycycline is particularly useful against atypical and tick-borne pathogens, including several Rickettsia species, and the lecture names it the first-line treatment for Rickettsiae (and for Lyme disease).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aminopenicillins are not the lecture's first-line agent for rickettsial infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aztreonam acts only on aerobic gram-negative bacteria and has no role for Rickettsia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cephalexin is a first-generation cephalosporin aimed at streptococci and staphylococci, not Rickettsia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aminoglycosides target aerobic gram-negative bacilli and are ineffective against atypical pathogens.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and indications-2 β-lactams and 30s Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man receives gentamicin for a gram-negative bacteremia. Which of the following best describes how this drug acts at the molecular level?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding to D-Ala-D-Ala termini, blocking cell wall polymer growth

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binding to penicillin-binding proteins, blocking cell wall cross-links

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibition of DNA gyrase, blocking supercoiling of bacterial DNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Irreversible binding to the 30S subunit, causing mRNA misreading

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reversible binding to the 50S subunit, blocking peptide transfer

explanation.summary: Aminoglycosides bind irreversibly to the 30S ribosomal subunit, causing mRNA misreading and inhibiting protein synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside. Aminoglycosides bind irreversibly to the 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of mRNA and inhibition of bacterial protein synthesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: That describes vancomycin, a cell wall agent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: That is the mechanism of β-lactams, not aminoglycosides.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aminoglycosides inhibit protein synthesis, not DNA replication.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aminoglycosides act on the 30S, not the 50S, subunit, and their binding is irreversible.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and indications-2 β-lactams and 30s Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman has a liver abscess that grows mixed aerobic and anaerobic flora. A student proposes gentamicin as the only agent. Which of the following best explains why gentamicin would fail against the anaerobic organisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anaerobes inactivate it with plasmid-encoded β-lactamases

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anaerobes lack the 30S ribosomal subunit it binds to

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anaerobes pump it out through constitutive efflux systems

choices.label: D
choices.text: Drug entry into cells needs oxygen-dependent transport

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires an acidic environment to cross the cell wall

explanation.summary: Aminoglycosides are ineffective against anaerobes because their uptake into bacteria requires oxygen-dependent transport.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aminoglycosides are primarily effective against aerobic gram-negative bacilli. They are ineffective against anaerobic organisms because oxygen-dependent transport is required to carry the drug into bacterial cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: β-lactamases degrade β-lactams, not aminoglycosides.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bacteria, including anaerobes, have 30S subunits; the problem is getting the drug inside the cell.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The lecture's explanation is failed uptake, not efflux.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The lecture attributes the failure to oxygen-dependent uptake, not to pH.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and indications-2 β-lactams and 30s Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has dysuria and urinary frequency. Urine culture grows a gram-negative organism that does not produce β-lactamase, and her physician plans oral amoxicillin, expecting the organism to fall within its intrinsic gram-negative spectrum. Which of the following organisms is most consistent with that plan?

explanation.summary: Aminopenicillin gram-negative coverage is remembered as HENPEK, which includes Proteus mirabilis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Amoxicillin and ampicillin cover selected gram-negative organisms remembered as HENPEK: Haemophilus influenzae, E. coli, Neisseria, Proteus mirabilis, Enterococcus, and Klebsiella pneumoniae. They do not reliably cover Pseudomonas or ESBL producers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acinetobacter is not among the aminopenicillin gram-negative organisms (HENPEK).
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aminopenicillins do not reliably cover ESBL-producing Enterobacterales.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aminopenicillins do not provide reliable coverage against Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serratia is listed under piperacillin-tazobactam and aminoglycoside coverage, not the HENPEK aminopenicillin list.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and indications-2 β-lactams and 30s Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man presents with fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, and confusion. CSF shows a neutrophilic pleocytosis with low glucose, and the Gram stain is not yet available. Which of the following empiric regimens is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: In meningitis patients over 50, ampicillin is added to ceftriaxone and vancomycin to cover Listeria.
explanation.whyCorrect: The common bacterial causes of meningitis are S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, and H. influenzae, covered by ceftriaxone with or without vancomycin. Patients over 50 also have a higher rate of Listeria monocytogenes, so ampicillin is added: ampicillin, ceftriaxone, and vancomycin.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Aztreonam has no gram-positive activity and this combination does not include Listeria coverage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Doxycycline adds atypical coverage, not the Listeria coverage that ampicillin provides in this age group.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This covers the common meningitis organisms but omits ampicillin, which is needed for Listeria in patients over 50.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This is not the lecture's meningitis regimen and lacks ampicillin for Listeria.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and indications-2 β-lactams and 30s Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man receiving intravenous vancomycin for MRSA osteomyelitis develops a catheter-associated urinary tract infection. Which of the following organisms would his current antibiotic fail to cover?

explanation.summary: Vancomycin covers gram-positive bacteria (including MRSA) but has no gram-negative coverage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vancomycin does not cover gram-negative bacteria. E. coli is a gram-negative bacillus, so a new gram-negative infection would need a different agent; every other option is gram-positive.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Vancomycin is effective against gram-positive bacteria including MRSA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This is a gram-positive organism within vancomycin's spectrum.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This is a gram-positive organism within vancomycin's spectrum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This is a gram-positive organism within vancomycin's spectrum.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and indications-2 β-lactams and 30s Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman presents with fever and diffuse peritonitis from a perforated diverticulum. A mixed infection involving gram-negative, gram-positive, and anaerobic organisms is suspected, possibly including Pseudomonas aeruginosa. She has no risk factors for ESBL organisms. Which single agent is most appropriate as initial empiric therapy?

explanation.summary: Piperacillin-tazobactam's broad gram-positive, gram-negative, anaerobic, and antipseudomonal coverage makes it a common empiric choice for polymicrobial infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Piperacillin-tazobactam provides broad gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic coverage with activity against susceptible Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Because of that breadth it is commonly used as initial empiric therapy for suspected polymicrobial infections (though it is not reliable against ESBL producers).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aminopenicillins, even with clavulanate, do not reliably cover Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aztreonam has no gram-positive or anaerobic activity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ertapenem lacks coverage against Pseudomonas (and Enterococcus and Acinetobacter).
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aminoglycosides are ineffective against anaerobes and are not used alone for gram-positive infections.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and indications-2 β-lactams and 30s Inhibitors

questions.stem: A hospital changes its gentamicin protocol to give fewer, larger doses for gram-negative infections, aiming to optimize bacterial killing. Which pharmacodynamic parameter best predicts the bactericidal activity of this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Duration of infusion relative to dosing interval

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fraction of the dose excreted unchanged in urine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ratio of maximum concentration to the MIC

choices.label: D
choices.text: Time the free drug level stays above the MIC

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trough concentration just before the next dose

explanation.summary: Aminoglycosides show concentration-dependent killing, so Cmax:MIC predicts their activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aminoglycosides exhibit concentration-dependent killing (Cmax:MIC): higher peak concentrations produce greater antibacterial activity. Their post-antibiotic effect also suppresses growth after levels fall below the MIC.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Infusion duration is not the parameter the lecture links to aminoglycoside killing.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Renal elimination describes clearance, not antibacterial activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aminoglycosides show concentration-dependent, not time-dependent, killing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Higher peak concentrations, not troughs, drive aminoglycoside activity.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and indications-2 β-lactams and 30s Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 28-year-old wrestler has a fluctuant abscess on his thigh with surrounding erythema. After incision and drainage, culture grows methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. He is well enough for outpatient oral therapy. Which of the following is the most appropriate agent?

explanation.summary: Doxycycline is used for skin and soft tissue infections because its gram-positive coverage includes MRSA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tetracyclines are active against Staphylococcus including MRSA. Many skin and soft tissue infections, purulent or non-purulent, are treated with doxycycline for that reason, and doxycycline is used both inpatient and outpatient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adding clavulanate overcomes many β-lactamases but does not provide MRSA coverage.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aztreonam has no gram-positive activity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cephalexin targets streptococci and susceptible staphylococci but does not cover MRSA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Carbapenems cover many gram-positive organisms except MRSA, and ertapenem is not an oral agent.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and indications-2 β-lactams and 30s Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with a complicated urinary tract infection is started on oral ciprofloxacin. The drug rapidly kills the infecting Escherichia coli. Which of the following bacterial targets does this agent inhibit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aminoacyl-tRNA site of the 30S ribosomal subunit

choices.label: B
choices.text: DNA-dependent RNA polymerase of the bacterium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Penicillin-binding transpeptidases of the cell wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peptidyl transferase of the 50S ribosomal subunit

explanation.summary: Fluoroquinolones are bactericidal inhibitors of DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin are bactericidal and inhibit DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, enzymes needed for DNA replication, transcription and chromosome separation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking the 30S subunit describes a protein synthesis inhibitor, not a fluoroquinolone.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fluoroquinolones block the topoisomerases, not bacterial RNA polymerase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transpeptidase binding is the beta-lactam mechanism, not the fluoroquinolone one.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibition of the 50S subunit is not the fluoroquinolone mechanism; these drugs act on topoisomerases.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications-3 Fluoroquinolones and Sulfonamides

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a chronic foot wound has cultures that grow Pseudomonas aeruginosa. His physician wants an oral agent with reliable antipseudomonal activity. Which of the following is the most appropriate choice?

explanation.summary: Among fluoroquinolones, ciprofloxacin reliably covers Pseudomonas aeruginosa; moxifloxacin does not.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ciprofloxacin has strong activity against aerobic Gram-negative bacilli and is active against Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Unlike ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin, moxifloxacin does not provide reliable activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sulfacetamide is used in selected ophthalmic preparations, not for systemic Pseudomonas infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sulfadiazine is used in combination therapy for toxoplasmosis, not for Pseudomonas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TMP-SMX covers E. coli, K. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, P. mirabilis and CA-MRSA, but Pseudomonas is not part of its described spectrum.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications-3 Fluoroquinolones and Sulfonamides

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with dysuria and urinary frequency is prescribed moxifloxacin, and her symptoms persist despite adherence. A pharmacist explains that this drug is a poor choice for bladder infections. Which of the following best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It has no activity against aerobic Gram-negative bacilli

choices.label: B
choices.text: It has poor oral bioavailability after a single dose

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is chelated by the urea present in bladder urine

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is mostly cleared nonrenally and reaches low urine levels

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is restricted to parenteral use in hospitals

explanation.summary: Moxifloxacin is not used for UTI because it is eliminated nonrenally and does not concentrate in urine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Moxifloxacin undergoes mainly nonrenal elimination, so it does not concentrate in the urine and does not reach effective levels in the urinary tract.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Moxifloxacin retains activity against several Gram-negative pathogens; its problem in UTI is pharmacokinetic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fluoroquinolones generally have good oral bioavailability.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fluoroquinolone chelation occurs with polyvalent cations such as calcium, magnesium, iron and aluminum, not urea.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fluoroquinolones are well absorbed orally; route is not why moxifloxacin fails in UTI.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications-3 Fluoroquinolones and Sulfonamides

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man feels a sudden pop behind his ankle while climbing stairs and now cannot stand on his toes. One week earlier he began an oral antibiotic for a respiratory infection. Which of the following antibiotics was most likely prescribed?

explanation.summary: Tendon rupture is a fluoroquinolone warning, with risk rising after age 60.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fluoroquinolones carry a warning for tendon rupture, and the risk increases with age over 60. Levofloxacin is a respiratory fluoroquinolone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amoxicillin/clavulanate is a beta-lactam and does not carry this warning.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cephalexin is a beta-lactam and is not associated with the fluoroquinolone tendon warning.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TMP-SMX is not the class carrying the tendon rupture warning.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vancomycin is associated with red man syndrome, not tendon rupture.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications-3 Fluoroquinolones and Sulfonamides

questions.stem: A 24-year-old wrestler has a fluctuant skin abscess. After drainage, culture grows a community-associated methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus isolate. He is to be treated as an outpatient with an oral agent. Which of the following is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: TMP-SMX covers many community-associated MRSA isolates.
explanation.whyCorrect: TMP-SMX has activity against many community-associated MRSA isolates and is given orally.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amoxicillin/clavulanate is a beta-lactam and does not provide MRSA coverage.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ampicillin/sulbactam covers non-MRSA gram-positives only.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ceftriaxone is listed for gram-negative coverage, not MRSA coverage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Piperacillin/tazobactam is listed for gram-negative and pseudomonal coverage, not MRSA.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications-3 Fluoroquinolones and Sulfonamides

questions.stem: A clinician wants a fluoroquinolone for a patient with pneumococcal pneumonia. The agent should have the most enhanced activity against Gram-positive organisms, and the patient has no risk factors for Pseudomonas, which this agent does not reliably cover. Which of the following fits best?

explanation.summary: Moxifloxacin has the most enhanced Gram-positive (S. pneumoniae) activity but lacks reliable Pseudomonas coverage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Moxifloxacin has enhanced activity against Gram-positive organisms, particularly Streptococcus pneumoniae, and retains atypical and some Gram-negative activity, but it does not reliably cover Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ciprofloxacin has its greatest strength against aerobic Gram-negative bacilli and less reliable activity against S. pneumoniae.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Levofloxacin is also a respiratory fluoroquinolone, but moxifloxacin has the more enhanced Gram-positive activity, and levofloxacin may cover susceptible Pseudomonas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sulfadiazine is a sulfonamide used for toxoplasmosis, not a fluoroquinolone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TMP-SMX is a sulfonamide combination, not a fluoroquinolone.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications-3 Fluoroquinolones and Sulfonamides

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman has 3 days of dysuria, urgency and frequency without fever or flank tenderness. She had a severe rash with sulfa drugs in the past, and she has congenital long QT syndrome. Which of the following is the most appropriate empiric oral therapy?

explanation.summary: When TMP-SMX and fluoroquinolones are excluded, a beta-lactam such as amoxicillin/clavulanate or cephalexin can treat cystitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: TMP-SMX (first-line for cystitis) is excluded by her sulfa allergy, and fluoroquinolones cause QTc prolongation, so a beta-lactam such as amoxicillin/clavulanate or cephalexin is a good option.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fluoroquinolones prolong the QTc interval and should be avoided in long QT syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Levofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone and carries the QTc prolongation warning.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Moxifloxacin both prolongs the QTc and does not concentrate in urine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Her prior sulfa reaction rules out TMP-SMX even though it is often first-line for cystitis.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications-3 Fluoroquinolones and Sulfonamides

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman takes an antacid containing magnesium and aluminum with every meal. She is started on oral ciprofloxacin for pyelonephritis and takes each dose with breakfast, but her infection fails to improve. Which of the following best explains the treatment failure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alkaline gastric contents inactivate the drug's structure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chelation by polyvalent cations lowers drug absorption

choices.label: C
choices.text: Displacement from plasma proteins boosts its clearance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased renal tubular secretion shortens the half-life

choices.label: E
choices.text: Induction of hepatic enzymes accelerates drug breakdown

explanation.summary: Polyvalent cations (Ca, Mg, Fe, Al) chelate fluoroquinolones and reduce absorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fluoroquinolone absorption is reduced by chelation with polyvalent cations such as calcium, magnesium, iron and aluminum.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The interaction is binding (chelation) by cations, not pH inactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Protein-binding displacement is not the described fluoroquinolone interaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antacids reduce fluoroquinolone absorption; they do not speed renal clearance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The lecture identifies cation chelation, not enzyme induction, as the absorption problem.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications-3 Fluoroquinolones and Sulfonamides

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man in the intensive care unit develops ventilator-associated pneumonia, and sputum grows Pseudomonas. Which of the following regimens provides gram-negative and pseudomonal coverage?

explanation.summary: For Pseudomonas: cefepime, piperacillin/tazobactam or a carbapenem other than ertapenem.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cefepime, piperacillin/tazobactam and carbapenems other than ertapenem provide gram-negative and pseudomonal coverage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ampicillin/sulbactam is listed only for non-MRSA gram-positive coverage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ceftriaxone gives gram-negative coverage but does not cover Pseudomonas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ertapenem is the carbapenem exception that does not cover Pseudomonas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Moxifloxacin does not provide reliable activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

questions.stem: A healthy 23-year-old woman has 2 days of dysuria and urinary frequency with no fever, flank pain or drug allergies. She is not pregnant. Which of the following is often used as first-line oral therapy for her condition?

explanation.summary: TMP-SMX is often first-line for uncomplicated acute cystitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: First-line treatment of acute cystitis is often sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim; ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin are alternatives.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ampicillin/sulbactam is listed for non-MRSA gram-positive coverage, not first-line cystitis therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Moxifloxacin does not concentrate in urine and is not used for UTIs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Piperacillin/tazobactam is a broad antipseudomonal agent, not first-line for uncomplicated cystitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vancomycin is an MRSA agent, not first-line therapy for cystitis caused by gram-negative rods.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man has fever, headache and ring-enhancing brain lesions attributed to Toxoplasma gondii. He is started on a combination regimen that includes a sulfonamide. Which of the following agents is this sulfonamide?

explanation.summary: Sulfadiazine is part of combination therapy for toxoplasmosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sulfonamides also act on selected protozoa; sulfadiazine is used as part of combination therapy for toxoplasmosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone, not a sulfonamide.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Levofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone, not a sulfonamide.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Silver sulfadiazine is a topical agent used for burn wounds.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sulfacetamide is used in selected ophthalmic preparations.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man is given ciprofloxacin for community-acquired pneumonia. Which of the following potential pathogens is least reliably covered by this choice?

explanation.summary: Ciprofloxacin is weak against S. pneumoniae, so respiratory fluoroquinolones are preferred for it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ciprofloxacin has limited gram-positive coverage and less reliable activity against Streptococcus pneumoniae than the respiratory fluoroquinolones.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ciprofloxacin has potent activity against H. influenzae.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ciprofloxacin is strong against aerobic Gram-negative bacilli such as Klebsiella.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ciprofloxacin has potent activity against M. catarrhalis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ciprofloxacin is active against Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

questions.stem: A pharmacology student compares clindamycin, linezolid, macrolides, chloramphenicol, and streptogramins, all of which bind the large (50S) ribosomal subunit. What is the general effect of this drug group on susceptible bacteria?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bactericidal lysis of the cell wall

explanation.summary: 50S inhibitors (macrolides, clindamycin, linezolid, chloramphenicol, streptogramins) block protein synthesis and are generally bacteriostatic.
explanation.whyCorrect: Agents targeting the 50S subunit inhibit bacterial protein synthesis and are generally bacteriostatic: they stop growth rather than lyse the cell.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Membrane disruption is not the mechanism of this group, which is generally bacteriostatic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA gyrase inhibition is the fluoroquinolone mechanism, not a ribosomal one.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cell wall lysis is the action of beta-lactams and vancomycin, not 50S inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Folate synthesis blockade is not how 50S inhibitors act; they block protein synthesis.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old college student has 10 days of low-grade fever, headache, and a dry cough. A nasopharyngeal PCR panel is positive for Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Which of the following agents provides the most appropriate coverage for this organism?

explanation.summary: Macrolides cover the atypical respiratory pathogens Mycoplasma, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and Legionella.
explanation.whyCorrect: Macrolides such as azithromycin provide important activity against atypical respiratory pathogens, including Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and Legionella pneumophila.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Aztreonam covers susceptible aerobic Gram-negative organisms, not atypical pathogens.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cephalexin is a beta-lactam aimed at Gram-positive skin pathogens and does not cover atypical organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Clindamycin covers aerobic Gram-positive cocci and anaerobes, not atypical respiratory pathogens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Linezolid is a Gram-positive agent (MRSA, VRE) and is not used for atypical pneumonia.

questions.stem: A clinician is considering clindamycin for a patient with a soft tissue infection. Which of the following organism groups does this drug reliably cover?

explanation.summary: Clindamycin covers aerobic Gram-positive cocci and anaerobes above the diaphragm, but not aerobic Gram-negative bacilli or Enterococcus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Clindamycin is active against many aerobic Gram-positive cocci and several anaerobes, particularly for infections above the diaphragm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clindamycin does not provide reliable activity against aerobic Gram-negative bacilli.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The lecture frames clindamycin's anaerobic role as infections above the diaphragm, not below it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Clindamycin is not effective against Enterococcus species.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VRE is an Enterococcus, which clindamycin does not cover; linezolid is the VRE agent.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man in the intensive care unit develops bacteremia. Blood cultures grow Enterococcus faecium that is resistant to vancomycin. Which of the following agents is most appropriate for this isolate?

explanation.summary: Linezolid covers vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VRE).
explanation.whyCorrect: Linezolid is active against Gram-positive organisms including MRSA and vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VRE).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amoxicillin does not provide reliable activity against VRE.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Azithromycin is not a standard treatment for VRE.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aztreonam covers susceptible aerobic Gram-negative organisms and has no Gram-positive activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Clindamycin is not effective against Enterococcus species, including VRE.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman has a diabetic foot wound. Culture grows MRSA together with Escherichia coli. She is started on linezolid alone. Which part of the culture result is left untreated by this regimen?

explanation.summary: Linezolid is a Gram-positive-only agent (MRSA, VRE) with no Gram-negative coverage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Linezolid's coverage resembles vancomycin's: Gram-positive organisms including MRSA and VRE. It provides no Gram-negative coverage, so the Gram-negative bacillus is untreated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Linezolid does cover the MRSA isolate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Linezolid has no Gram-negative activity, so one isolate remains uncovered.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The question concerns the reported isolates; the Gram-negative E. coli is the gap.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Linezolid is active against MRSA, so this isolate is covered.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy in North Carolina has fever, headache, and a rash that began on the wrists and ankles a week after a tick bite. Rickettsia rickettsii infection is suspected. Which of the following is the first-line treatment?

explanation.summary: Doxycycline is first-line for Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever (Rickettsia rickettsii).
explanation.whyCorrect: Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever, caused by Rickettsia rickettsii, is treated first-line with doxycycline, the first-line agent for most tick-borne infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aztreonam covers aerobic Gram-negative organisms and is not used for rickettsial disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cephalexin is not a treatment for rickettsial disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Clindamycin is not used for Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Linezolid is a Gram-positive agent, not therapy for tick-borne rickettsiae.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man who smokes presents with high fever, confusion, diarrhea, and pneumonia two weeks after staying at a hotel with a contaminated cooling tower. A urine antigen test confirms Legionella. Which of the following is a first-line treatment?

explanation.summary: Legionnaires' disease is treated with azithromycin or levofloxacin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Legionnaires' disease is treated with azithromycin or levofloxacin. Levofloxacin is a respiratory fluoroquinolone with this indication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aztreonam is not a treatment for Legionnaires' disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cephalexin does not cover atypical organisms such as Legionella.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Clindamycin covers Gram-positive cocci and anaerobes, not Legionella.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Linezolid covers Gram-positive organisms only and is not used for Legionnaires' disease.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old otherwise healthy man is diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia and is well enough for outpatient care. He had hives and wheezing after amoxicillin as a child, and a prior ECG showed a prolonged QT interval. Which empiric regimen is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: In a healthy CAP outpatient with penicillin allergy and QT prolongation, doxycycline is the appropriate empiric choice.
explanation.whyCorrect: Healthy outpatients with CAP may receive amoxicillin(/clavulanate), doxycycline, or a macrolide. Penicillin allergy excludes amoxicillin/clavulanate and macrolides raise QT-prolongation risk, leaving doxycycline.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A penicillin allergy makes amoxicillin/clavulanate inappropriate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Macrolides increase the risk of QT prolongation, which this patient already has.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ciprofloxacin is not a respiratory fluoroquinolone because of poor S. pneumoniae activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Clindamycin does not cover atypical pathogens or H. influenzae and is not a standard CAP option here.

questions.stem: A resident proposes ciprofloxacin for a patient with community-acquired pneumonia. The attending explains that ciprofloxacin is not grouped with the respiratory fluoroquinolones. What is the main reason?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Poor oral absorption from the small intestine

explanation.summary: Ciprofloxacin is not a respiratory fluoroquinolone because of poor Streptococcus pneumoniae activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ciprofloxacin is not considered a respiratory fluoroquinolone primarily because it has poor activity against Streptococcus pneumoniae, a common CAP pathogen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This is not the reason ciprofloxacin is excluded from the respiratory group.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The stated limitation is pneumococcal coverage, not Legionella.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The defining weakness is against S. pneumoniae, not Mycoplasma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Absorption is not the reason given; the issue is the pneumococcal gap.

questions.stem: Linezolid and the streptogramin quinupristin/dalfopristin both treat MRSA and are used only for Gram-positive organisms. Their coverage most closely resembles that of which of the following drugs?

explanation.summary: Linezolid and streptogramins have vancomycin-like Gram-positive coverage including MRSA.
explanation.whyCorrect: The coverage of linezolid and streptogramins is similar to vancomycin: Gram-positive organisms including MRSA, with no Gram-negative activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Azithromycin's hallmark is atypical respiratory coverage, not MRSA coverage.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aztreonam is the opposite: aerobic Gram-negative coverage with no Gram-positive activity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone, not a Gram-positive-only agent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Doxycycline is the first-line agent for tick-borne atypical bacteria, a different profile.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old landscaper is prescribed doxycycline for an infection. Which counseling point is most important to give before he returns to outdoor work?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Check the ECG for QT changes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Take it only with grapefruit juice

explanation.summary: Doxycycline causes photosensitivity; counsel sun protection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Doxycycline can cause photosensitive reactions, so patients should be advised to protect themselves from the sun.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Penicillin avoidance relates to a penicillin allergy, not to doxycycline therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: QT prolongation is the concern raised for macrolides, not doxycycline.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This is unrelated counseling and does not describe a doxycycline adverse effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This is not a counseling point tied to doxycycline in the lecture.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with chronic heart failure and diabetes has community-acquired pneumonia and will be treated as an outpatient. He has no drug allergies and a normal QT interval. Which regimen fits the broader therapy recommended for outpatients with comorbidities?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A beta-lactam combined with a macrolide

explanation.summary: Comorbid CAP outpatients may need a beta-lactam plus a macrolide (or doxycycline), or a respiratory fluoroquinolone.
explanation.whyCorrect: Outpatients with certain comorbidities may need broader therapy: a beta-lactam combined with a macrolide or doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone.

whyWrongByChoice.B: This pairing does not cover atypical pathogens and is not a CAP regimen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ciprofloxacin is not a respiratory fluoroquinolone because of poor S. pneumoniae activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Clindamycin lacks atypical and reliable Gram-negative coverage for CAP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both are Gram-positive-focused and leave H. influenzae and atypicals uncovered.
